request.job_description: We are hiring a Data Engineer to own our batch and streaming data pipelines and the data quality framework that supports analytics, ML features, and finance reporting. You will design and operate pipelines on a cloud warehouse and a Kafka-based streaming platform, define SLAs, build automated data quality checks, and partner with analysts and product teams. Requirements: 3+ years building production pipelines, strong SQL and Python, experience with orchestration (Airflow or similar), streaming (Kafka/Flink/Spark Streaming), and a track record of improving reliability and data trust.

transcript.question: Walk me through a pipeline you designed end to end and the key design decisions you made.
transcript.answer: Sure. I built our order events pipeline. Source was a Postgres OLTP database with about 40 million order-related rows changing per day. I used Debezium CDC into Kafka, then a Spark Structured Streaming job writing to Delta tables in a bronze layer, with dbt models building silver and gold layers in the warehouse on a 15-minute cadence. I considered just doing nightly full extracts, which was what we had, but the finance team needed intraday numbers and the extracts were putting 20 minutes of heavy read load on the primary. CDC dropped that load to near zero on the primary. The trade-off was operational complexity: we had to handle schema evolution and out-of-order events. I handled that with a schema registry using backward-compatible rules and by deduplicating on primary key plus the LSN, keeping the latest version. I also made the bronze layer append-only so we could replay from any point, which saved us twice later.

transcript.question: How do you decide between batch and streaming for a given use case, and where have you gotten that wrong?
transcript.answer: I start with the freshness requirement the consumer actually needs, not what they ask for. People say real time, but when I ask what decision changes if the data is five minutes old versus an hour old, often nothing changes. Streaming costs more in infra and on-call burden, so I default to micro-batch unless latency under a few minutes matters. I got it wrong once: I built a streaming aggregation for marketing attribution that ran 24/7 on a cluster costing roughly 4k a month, and the dashboard was only looked at each morning. I replaced it with an hourly dbt incremental model and cut the cost by about 85 percent with no complaints. On the other side, for fraud signals we needed under 30 seconds end to end, so I used Flink with keyed state and exactly-once checkpointing to Kafka, and I tuned checkpoint intervals to 30 seconds to balance recovery time against overhead.

transcript.question: Tell me about how you've built data quality checks. What did you measure and what changed?
transcript.answer: When I joined, there was no systematic testing, and analysts found bad data before we did. I introduced layered checks. At ingestion: schema validation and row count anomaly detection compared to a trailing 4-week same-weekday baseline. In transformation: dbt tests for uniqueness, not-null, and referential integrity, plus custom tests like revenue reconciliation between the orders table and the payments ledger within 0.1 percent. I made critical checks block the DAG and non-critical ones alert only, because early on everything blocked and we got alert fatigue. I tracked incidents where a stakeholder found the issue first; that went from about 9 a quarter to 1 over two quarters. I also published a data quality dashboard with freshness and test pass rates per table so owners were visible.

transcript.question: Describe a production incident you owned. What happened and what did you do afterwards?
transcript.answer: A schema change upstream renamed a column without notice, and our CDC consumer began writing nulls into a field used by the revenue dashboard. I was on call. An alert on null rate fired within 10 minutes, I paused the downstream dbt runs to stop propagation, then confirmed the cause from the schema registry history. Because bronze was append-only, I patched the mapping and replayed about six hours of events, and the gold tables were corrected in roughly 90 minutes. I told the finance lead right away in the incident channel with an estimate for correction, rather than waiting until I had it fixed. Afterwards I wrote a postmortem, and we added a contract test in the producer team's CI that fails on breaking schema changes, and I got their agreement to a deprecation window of two weeks. We haven't had a repeat in the year since.

transcript.question: How do you work with analysts and other stakeholders when priorities conflict?
transcript.answer: I try to make the trade-offs visible. We had a quarter where finance wanted a new reconciliation pipeline and the ML team wanted feature backfills, and both claimed top priority. I wrote a one-page comparison with effort estimates, who was blocked, and the risk of delay, then walked the two leads and my manager through it. Finance had a regulatory deadline, so that went first, and I gave the ML team a committed date for the backfill and a smaller interim extract so they weren't fully blocked. I also hold a short office hours slot weekly with analysts, which reduced ad hoc Slack requests noticeably, and I document table definitions in the catalog so they can self-serve.
